sections.text: He attains Peace, into whom desires flow as rivers into the ocean, which though brimming with water remains ever the same; not he whom desire carries away.
He attains Peace who, giving up desire, moves through the world without aspiration, possessing nothing which he can call his own, and free from pride.
एषा ब्राह्मी स्थितिः पार्थ नैनां प्राप्य विमुह्यति।

O Arjuna! This is the state of the Self, the Supreme Spirit, to which if a man once attain, it shall never be taken from him. Even at the time of leaving the body, he will remain firmly enthroned there, and will become one with the Eternal.

We had been discussing Chapter 2, Sankhya Yoga, the Yoga of Knowledge. We are coming to the end of chapter two, and we will be discussing the last three verses today, then well move on to chapter three, Karma Yoga, the Yoga of Action. What we have learned so far in chapter two is essentially the whole summary of Bhagavad Gita -- all the ideas and the basic philosophy of Bhagavad Gita are summarized in chapter two.
The most important verse in the first section was verse 7, where Arjuna said, karpanya doshopahatah svabhavah -- my nature is overwhelmed by the taint of miserliness or weakness, and I do not know what is right and wrong for me. I dont know what is my Dharma. Dharma sammudha chetasah -- my Buddhi does not tell me right now what is my right Dharma at this time. Shishyas teham -- so he admits: I need guidance.
I need someone to tell me what is right. Therefore, tell me definitively, without any wavering, what is right for me. So the first section gives us a condition we sometimes face in life: we are completely overwhelmed by the situation and we cannot see what is right and wrong for us.
But where we differ from Arjuna is that our ego doesnt give us that humility to say, Im completely confused, I am your student, please guide me. Even at the point of confusion and delusion, we try to hang on to our ego and try to solve our problems ourselves. And therefore we cant see how to get out of this problem. Because we are in the problem, we need to surrender to someone who can see it from outside, have complete faith in his advice and guidance, and say, Im going to follow whatever you tell me, just tell me. But what we typically do is carry our ego to whoever we are seeking advice from.
We say, Look, okay, but what does he know? My problem only I know. Thats why we fail to get the benefit of advice. So Bhagavan did not say anything in chapter one because he didnt see that Arjuna was ready yet., giving advice to the wrong person at the wrong time can do more harm than help. If somebody is not ready to take the advice and you say, Let me tell you, my son -- he has to be ready before you can tell him what is right for him.
So the first thing we have seen is that when you reach a point of complete confusion in your life, you have to surrender. In this case, if nothing else, surrender to your own conscience, which is Bhagavan, and say, Give me guidance. Tell me, I dont know. My intellect cannot come to the conclusion of what is right or wrong.
And then we have seen all the guidance Bhagavan gave. He first changes Arjunas paradigm of what he thinks he is. You are not who you think you are.
This limited being which you have considered yourself to be is not really you. This is just your equipment. This body, mind, and intellect which I currently consider to be me is actually nothing but my equipment.
So if I can realize that this is something which is mine and cannot be me, then I will be able to realize who I truly am and get the benefit of that wisdom. So Bhagavan changed his paradigm and said: you are that imperishable being. And then we have seen the explanation -- just as you change your clothes, you will change the body as well, but you remain the same.
Just as you changed from childhood to youth to old age, from this life youll move on to the next life. The advice given by Bhagavan in verse 38 is how to live life: Sukha duhkhe same kritva labhalabho jayajayau, tato yuddhaya yujyasva naivam papam avapsyasi. Here is how you should live your life: not a life of inaction, not a life of complete detachment from your duties, but complete detachment from whats happening to you.
Have that understanding that all things are transitory, finite in nature and in time-space. So sukha duhkhe same kritva -- you remain the same whether experiencing sukha or duhkha. I will still experience them differently -- one will be pleasurable, one will be painful.
But I experience both while keeping in mind that this is just a passing phase, a finite experience. How do I keep my balance? Victory and defeat in our life -- we are constantly winning and losing. Were winning an argument, we are winning a negotiation, we are losing a deal.
Marketing people teach you that everyone is selling something. You may not consider yourself a salesman, but you are selling something to somebody -- selling your idea to your spouse about which vacation to take. You have to sell your idea first.
So youre constantly selling and marketing and winning and losing in life, and you need to keep your balance. Just as you dont really get upset when you lose your argument within the family -- sometimes we do, but youre not supposed to because you understand we are still one family -- in the same way, when I lose or win out in the world, I should have the same equanimity. Others are going to win sometimes.
The law of probability tells me I cannot have 100% success. As I told you, in our industry we ask, what is the hit rate -- how many proposals are submitted and how many have we won? Now that hit rate is not really entirely dependent on you; its partly the law of probabilities. I know if I submit 10 proposals, Ill win at least one of them.
It is a law of probability. So I have to be prepared nine times to be disappointed that somebody else was better than me. But that one time when I win, Im so ecstatic -- I am the best. The other nine times, I will be miserable.
But no -- you have to be the same in all 10 times. Bhagavan said the operative word is: you just engage in this battle of life. You cant run away from it.
And theres a guarantee -- you will not incur any sin in doing your duty with this attitude. No matter what the outcome is, you are not incurring any wrong impressions on your mind. And then the last section we have seen is the Sthita Prajna.
In the end, Arjuna said, if someone achieves this, how do I recognize him? So verse 55 gives a short definition: prajahati yada kaman sarvan partha manogatan, atmany evatmana tushtah sthitaprajnas tadochyate. How do I become that person who is in a blissful mood all the time? Because you are saying yuddhaya yujyasva -- you want me to engage in the battle. Typically what we say is, This is too painful an environment.
I need to leave this environment. Bhagavan said no, you cant leave. Its part of your duty. You have to engage yourself in this battle of life and still remain equanimous, stable, blissful.
How? He said Prajahati yada kaman sarvan manogatan. He didnt say to give up all desires. Desires cannot go away completely.
Manogatan means fabricated by my mind -- something which I really dont need but I think I have to have. One thing I learned in all the training we go through in the corporate world -- one of the trainings I did was Negotiate to Win. They have an exercise about Honest Abdullahs shop in Pakistan, and you are an American tourist going to negotiate for an antique piece. The first thing the American does is say, Oh thats great, I got to have it. Once Abdullah hears I got to have it, he knows hes got you, and then hes going to start from the highest price he can imagine, then come down slightly, and you think you have done well.
But if youre from India, what do you do? Well, I really dont need it, but I think, you know, Im here. Meena and I went to India last time at one of these historical places, and she said, I can buy it, but I dont really have space for this in my bag, so I cant really buy it. But if you give it to me for this price, Ill buy it. The guy said, So if I give you the lower price, youll have space in your bag? She said, No, I can only buy -- okay, I dont have space in my bag. So we worked the other way around: I really dont need it, but if you want to give it to me at that price, okay. So this is Manogatan -- desires fabricated by my mind. If I give up all the desires which are fabricated by my mind -- not my genuine needs -- thats the key.
I have a desire to fulfill my needs: Im thirsty and I want a glass of water, that is one thing. But if I have to buy a Perrier just because its a status symbol, well, thats my Manogatan desire. So Bhagavan said that if you give up all the Manogatan desires and just be happy with whatever you come across.
Atmany evatmana tushtah. Fulfilling my desires is not giving me happiness or joy -- it is just fulfilling my needs. But I am always satisfied in myself, by myself, with who I am and where I am.
Atmany evatmana tushtah sthitaprajnas tadochyate. That is the definition of Sthita Prajna. Not that he is not working in this world, or that he is a sanyasi in the Himalayas.
He is working in this world but is satisfied in himself, where he is. He is not getting jealous by reading Forbes magazine -- All these people are making all this money and what am I doing here? When I am not disturbed by the outside world, that outside world cannot create unnecessary desires in my mind. Then I am a Sthita Prajna.
So we have gone through the whole characteristics of the Sthita Prajna -- he works in this world in a very intelligent way. Thats an intelligent way of living. He does not live life in a chaotic way, whereas we live life somewhat prompted by our instincts.
We go to the mall with no plan to buy X, Y, or Z. But just because Im there and I see something, I keep saying, Maybe I need that, maybe I should have that because its on sale. Thats because I never really defined what will make me happy. So what does the Sthita Prajna do? He lives an intelligent life.
He does not expose himself to those temptations. As soon as he sees there are temptations, he withdraws his senses, like the tortoise. So hes always protecting himself from getting undue impressions which are not necessary.
And thats how he lives an intelligent life, maintaining his state of equanimity. And then the last four verses tell us the difference between us and him. Right now Im completely aware of the world of objects.
And there are myriads of objects in this world. And Im seeking happiness in those objects, constantly planning how can I get happiness from them.

The chapter concludes with the beautiful ocean analogy in verse 70: He attains Peace, into whom desires flow as rivers into the ocean, which though brimming with water remains ever the same; not he whom desire carries away. The ocean receives all rivers yet remains unchanged - full but not overflowing, deep and still. Similarly, experiences and desires come to the sage but do not disturb his fundamental peace. He is already full.
Verse 71 summarizes the path: He attains Peace who, giving up desire, moves through the world without aspiration, possessing nothing which he can call his own, and free from pride. Three qualities: Nishprihaha (without craving), Nirmamaha (without mine-ness), and Nirahankaraha (without ego). And the final verse 72 declares: This is the state of the Self, the Supreme Spirit, to which if a man once attain, it shall never be taken from him. Even at the time of leaving the body, he will remain firmly enthroned there, and will become one with the Eternal.
As Chapter 2 ends, reflect on its complete teaching: You are not the body but the eternal Self. Perform your duty without attachment to results. Cultivate equanimity toward pleasure and pain. Control the senses through higher focus. Free yourself from the tyranny of likes and dislikes. Become like the ocean - full within yourself, receiving all experiences without being disturbed. Today, choose one of these teachings to focus on. Which resonates most with your current situation? That is your entry point into the practical wisdom of the Gita.
